prompt: A manufacturing plant's Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) dropped from a target of 78% to an actual 65% over the last month. Diagnose the deviation using the OEE components given and identify the priority driver to fix first.
context: OEE = Availability x Performance x Quality. This month: Availability 88% (target 92%), Performance 79% (target 86%), Quality 94% (target 98%). Maintenance log shows 3 unplanned changeover-related stoppages averaging 40 minutes each, tied to a new SKU introduced this month. Line operators report the new SKU runs at a slower validated cycle time than the legacy SKU it partially replaced.

binaryCriteria.description: Explicitly breaks the OEE gap into the Availability, Performance, and Quality components rather than treating OEE as a single unexplained number.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer does not reference the three components and their target-vs-actual gaps.

binaryCriteria.description: Identifies Performance (79% vs 86% target) as the largest relative decline and the priority driver, linking it to the new SKU's slower cycle time.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer prioritizes Availability/maintenance stoppages as the main driver ahead of the cycle-time issue, or ignores the SKU cycle-time detail.

binaryCriteria.description: Uses the specific evidence given (new SKU, slower validated cycle time, changeover stoppages) rather than generic manufacturing-efficiency platitudes.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the recommendation could apply to any OEE problem without referencing the SKU-specific evidence.

goldNotes: A strong answer decomposes OEE into its three multiplicative components and identifies which component degraded the most in relative terms, not just which has the biggest absolute point gap — Performance dropped from 86% to 79% (7pp, ~8% relative decline) and Availability from 92% to 88% (4pp, ~4% relative decline); Quality is closest to target (94% vs 98%, 4pp/~4%). A rigorous answer should note Performance is the largest relative decline and tie it directly to the new SKU's slower validated cycle time — a specific, given causal link — rather than treating all three components as equally weighted or defaulting to "maintenance issues" (which affects Availability, a smaller driver here). It should recommend prioritizing cycle-time/changeover work tied to the new SKU as the first fix.
